_disclaimer: This knowledge base provides GENERAL, non-quantitative agronomic background and management CATEGORIES for each disease, drawn from widely-documented plant pathology / IPM (Integrated Pest Management) principles and the disease descriptions already present in this project's own dataset documentation (README.md, Annotation Protocol.pdf). It deliberately contains NO pesticide/fungicide product names, dosages, concentrations, or application frequencies, because none were supplied with the project materials -- inventing those would be unsafe and scientifically indefensible. Every class's 'treatment' field is explicitly marked as requiring authoritative validation before any real-world use. This file must be reviewed and completed by a qualified agricultural extension officer or plant pathologist (e.g. via the Bangladesh Rice Research Institute / BRRI, or the Department of Agricultural Extension) before being used for real farming decisions.

Healthy.description: The leaf shows no visually detectable disease symptoms in the analyzed image.
symptoms: No lesions, spots, streaks, or discoloration typical of the 5 diseases in this system
management: Continue routine field monitoring for early symptom detection.
Maintain balanced fertilization and irrigation practices appropriate to the crop growth stage.
A single 'Healthy' prediction on one image/region is not a field-level guarantee -- keep monitoring other plants and later growth stages.
prevention: Preventive care generally applies across all diseases below (resistant varieties, field sanitation, balanced fertilization, proper water management).

Blast.description: One of the most economically damaging rice diseases worldwide; affects leaves, nodes, and panicles.
symptoms: Gray-white lesion centers with brown margins
Lesions may coalesce under severe pressure
management: Favor resistant/tolerant rice varieties where locally available.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization, particularly late top-dressing -- high N is a well-documented risk factor that increases blast susceptibility.
Maintain field sanitation: remove and destroy infected residue and volunteer rice plants between seasons.
Monitor closely during prolonged humid/cloudy/wet conditions, which favor spore production and spread.
treatment: NEEDS_AUTHORITATIVE_VALIDATION -- no specific fungicide product, dosage, concentration, or application-frequency data was supplied with this project's source materials. Consult a licensed agricultural extension officer (e.g. BRRI / Department of Agricultural Extension, Bangladesh) or a validated regional plant-protection guideline before applying any fungicide.
prevention: Avoid overly dense planting to improve canopy airflow and reduce humidity buildup.
Diversify/rotate varieties across seasons where feasible to reduce pathogen adaptation pressure.

Brown Spot.description: Historically linked to nutrient-stressed soils (notably the Bengal famine of 1943); affects leaves and grains.
symptoms: Can occur at very high density on a single leaf
Highest average lesion count per image among the diseases in this dataset
management: Correct soil fertility issues, particularly potassium deficiency, which is classically associated with Brown Spot severity.
Maintain field sanitation: remove infected crop residue.
Favor resistant/tolerant varieties where available.
Avoid moisture stress (both drought and waterlogging) where possible.
treatment: NEEDS_AUTHORITATIVE_VALIDATION -- no specific fungicide/seed-treatment product, dosage, concentration, or application-frequency data was supplied with this project's source materials. Consult a licensed agricultural extension officer or a validated regional plant-protection guideline before applying any treatment.
prevention: Use certified, disease-free (and where applicable, appropriately treated) seed.
Maintain balanced soil fertility, especially adequate potassium.
Avoid planting in known nutrient-poor or marginal soils without prior correction.

Leaf Smut.description: Generally considered a minor disease relative to Blast/Brown Spot/Sheath Blight, but can still reduce photosynthetic leaf area under heavy infection.
symptoms: Small black spots/streaks following leaf veins
Typical lesion size ~2-5 mm (smallest among the 5 diseases)
Pustules may rupture and release spores
management: Maintain field sanitation: remove and destroy infected leaf debris after harvest.
Avoid working in wet fields when pustules are visibly rupturing, to limit mechanical spore spread.
Favor resistant/tolerant varieties where available.
treatment: NEEDS_AUTHORITATIVE_VALIDATION -- no specific treatment product, dosage, concentration, or application-frequency data was supplied with this project's source materials. Consult a licensed agricultural extension officer before applying any treatment.
prevention: Avoid excessively dense canopies that retain leaf surface moisture.

Rice Tungro.causal_agent: Viral (Rice Tungro Bacilliform Virus + Rice Tungro Spherical Virus, transmitted by green leafhopper vectors)
Rice Tungro.description: A vector-borne viral disease -- unlike the fungal diseases in this dataset, there is no direct curative chemical treatment once a plant is infected; management is centered on vector control and preventing spread.
symptoms: Mottled, chlorotic (diffuse, non-discrete) patterns rather than sharply bounded lesions
Lowest average bounding-box count per image among the 5 diseases, consistent with its diffuse presentation
management: Because this is viral and vector-borne, management is about the leafhopper vector and infected plants, not a direct cure: monitor and manage green leafhopper populations using IPM principles (natural enemies, monitoring thresholds) rather than blanket insecticide use.
Promptly rogue (remove) clearly infected plants where practical, to reduce the local virus source.
Synchronize planting dates across a locality where feasible, to avoid continuous host availability that sustains vector populations.
treatment: NEEDS_AUTHORITATIVE_VALIDATION -- there is no direct chemical cure for an already-infected plant; any vector-control (insecticide) product, dosage, concentration, or application-frequency recommendation was NOT supplied with this project's source materials and must come from a licensed agricultural extension officer or validated regional guideline.
prevention: Use Tungro-tolerant/resistant varieties where locally available.
Synchronize community-level planting schedules to reduce vector bridging between seasons.
Manage leafhopper vector populations proactively through IPM rather than reactive spraying alone.

Sheath Blight.description: One of the major rice diseases, especially in densely planted, heavily fertilized, high-humidity conditions.
symptoms: Typically 1-3 cm or larger -- the largest average lesion size among the 5 diseases
management: Avoid excessive plant density and excessive nitrogen -- dense canopies plus high humidity are well-documented drivers of Sheath Blight spread.
Improve field drainage / water management; prolonged standing water combined with high humidity favors this pathogen.
Maintain field sanitation: remove infected stubble and residue after harvest.
treatment: NEEDS_AUTHORITATIVE_VALIDATION -- no specific fungicide product, dosage, concentration, or application-frequency data was supplied with this project's source materials. Consult a licensed agricultural extension officer or a validated regional plant-protection guideline before applying any fungicide.
prevention: Maintain proper plant spacing for canopy airflow.
Where feasible, avoid continuous flooding for extended periods.
